Why Central Asia matters for Washington

For three decades, the five post-Soviet republics of Central Asia were treated in Washington as a geopolitical backwater, a region to be managed rather than engaged.

That is changing. Uzbekistan, the most populous country in the region, has opened its economy, courted Western investors and signed a critical minerals agreement with the United States.

Officials in Tashkent say the partnership is about diversification rather than a choice between Moscow, Beijing and Washington.

The C5+1 format, once a talking shop, now has a working agenda on energy, water and transport corridors.
